summary: Round 2 of M4.8c. The three mechanism mutants round 1 named are now dead, measured individually in a copy of the staged bytes: pointer put->putIfAbsent fails 1 test, a hardcoded epoch in newestCheckpoint fails, and a pointer PUT issued once per stream fails thePointerADVANCESAndIsWrittenExactlyOncePerTrigger. The Invariants.readChain change is correct and does NOT weaken the checker: forcing the filter to exclude everything fails 15 tests, so over-filtering is pinned, and reusing the production allow-list rather than a second copy of the key grammar is the call M4.8b1's row requires. The cost shape holds -- a checkpoint is two PUTs per trigger, neither scaling with streams, pods, shards or indices, and discovery is stat+get whatever the history. Two things do not hold. (1) The new R1e paragraph on ChainReplay.newestCheckpoint asserts that nothing needs a chain-wide answer and that a recovering leader's OWN chain is where M4.9's bound applies; both are contradicted by M4.9's and M4.6e's own rows, and the misdirection lands on the one path this repository has measured as unbounded. (2) The pointer PUT's failure path is unreachable from any test, and the `written = true` ordering ADR-0034 records as a Consequence is a measured survivor. A smaller note, not filed as a finding: Invariants.readChain still builds a CommitLog -- a writer -- only for logPrefix(), with a LogKeys that answers the same question now sitting on the next line.

findings.blocks_reason: review.md `major-blocks`: on changes-requested a major finding blocks.
findings.title: The R1e javadoc says nothing needs a per-ancestor answer; M4.9's and M4.6e's rows both say something does, and it is the request rate this project exists to control
findings.detail: The new paragraph reads: 'IT ANSWERS FOR ONE EPOCH, the one passed. A recovering leader asks about ITS OWN chain, which is where M4.9's bound applies; a chain-wide answer across an ancestry would cost one stat per ancestor epoch, and nothing needs it -- crossing into a predecessor is M4.6e's path and inherits OFFSETS, not a replay bound.' Three claims in it are false against the tree. (a) 'A recovering leader asks about ITS OWN chain': every recovery holds a FRESH epoch -- M4.6e's row records that every restart, rolling deploy, TTL expiry and failed start burns one -- and ChainReplay's own javadoc says a new leader recovers its chain BEFORE opening it, so the own-epoch prefix holds no checkpoint at all at the moment recovery must be bounded. newestCheckpoint(store, prefix, ownEpoch) returns empty on every takeover. (b) 'nothing needs it': M4.9's row in backlog-notes.md states 'AND IT MUST BOUND THE CROSSING, not merely own-chain replay ... so the claim has to be true HERE rather than merely asserted there', and M4.6e's row states 'M4.8's checkpoints make it constant again'. The per-ancestor answer is exactly what M4.9 is required to build. (c) 'inherits OFFSETS, not a replay bound' is backwards as a reason: a Checkpoint IS offsets plus a sequence (ADR-0033), so a predecessor's checkpoint is precisely how the crossing gets bounded. The cost clause also compares in the wrong direction -- one stat per ancestor is the CHEAP side of what it dismisses.
findings.suggestion: State only what is checkable -- the method answers for the epoch passed, and bounding the crossing means calling it once per ancestor -- or delete the forward-looking clause outright, which is the remedy M4.8b1's row records after three drafts of the same kind of sentence were each measured wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.9 is implemented against the only prose at the call site. It calls newestCheckpoint for its own epoch, gets Optional.empty() at every takeover, and falls through to ChainReplay.replay, whose replayAncestry is transitive. Per-failover cost is then O(all commit-log entries ever written) and grows with the cluster's lifetime -- measured on M4.9's row at 17 GETs / 26 total requests for one prior term rising to 242/281 at sixteen, with LISTs and stats each growing per ancestor. That is a request rate scaling with history rather than with segments, AZs or nodes (non-negotiable 6), reintroduced by a javadoc that says the cheap fix is unnecessary. Nothing else in the tree contradicts the paragraph at the point a reader would look.

findings.blocks_reason: review.md `major-blocks`; the finding names the surviving mutation (`name-the-mutation`) and a concrete failure scenario (`failure-scenario`).
findings.title: The pointer PUT's failure path cannot be reached by any test, so the `written = true` ordering ADR-0034 records as a Consequence is a measured survivor
findings.detail: MEASURED in a copy of the staged bytes: moving `written = true;` from after the pointer PUT to before it leaves the whole :sequencer suite green (285 tests, BUILD SUCCESSFUL). The reason no test can reach it is in the fixture: RecordingBinStore.capture arms both injected failures only when `key.endsWith(".ckpt")`, and the pointer key ends in `/LATEST`, so failNextCheckpointPut and failEveryCheckpointPutUnchecked hit the seq-keyed putIfAbsent and stop there -- the pointer PUT never even executes under them. A checkpoint now costs two PUTs and only the first one's failure is exercised. RecordingBinStore's javadoc still calls failNextCheckpointPut 'the next CHECKPOINT PUT -- and only that one', which is no longer the whole of a checkpoint. ADR-0034 devotes a Consequence to this exact path ('A failed pointer write retries the whole checkpoint. The pointer is written BEFORE the writer marks the checkpoint written'), and the backlog row repeats it, so this is a recorded behavioural claim with nothing that would fail if it were untrue -- the same shape as R1a and as the four unpinned rationales M4.8b2's row catalogues.
findings.suggestion: Widen the arming predicate to every key a checkpoint writes (both `.ckpt` and the pointer), or add a `failNextPointerPut`, and drive one test through it asserting that the next trigger retries and the pointer advances. Small and local -- it does not mean the commit is too big under review.md `two-round-cap`.
findings.failure_scenario: A transient IOException on the pointer PUT after the seq-keyed putIfAbsent has landed. Under the surviving mutant the dirty flag is already cleared, so the IOException branch logs and nothing retries: ckpt/LATEST keeps the PREVIOUS checkpoint's bytes. On a quiet cluster, or any cluster below K deltas per T period, it keeps them for ever. Discovery then reports a stale sequence, and M4.9 resumes from it believing that is the newest checkpoint -- silent, and in the direction that replays a term the operator thinks is bounded.

findings.blocks_reason: Minor: review.md `minors-land`. Recorded here because it is the same misconception as R2a and is cheapest to fix in the same pass.
findings.title: The new 'pointer INSTEAD of the seq-keyed objects' alternative rationalises: it invents an M4.9 dependency that this same commit's other correction denies
findings.detail: The paragraph rejects the cheaper option partly on the ground that 'M4.9's bound is stated against a SEQUENCE -- "the newest checkpoint plus at most K deltas" -- which a single mutable object cannot evidence after the fact'. The pointer carries the checkpoint's own BYTES, and Checkpoint carries `sequence`, so M4.9's bound is served entirely from the pointer and needs no seq-keyed object at all. The R1d correction landing in the same commit says so in as many words at LogKeys.checkpointKeyFor: 'M4.9 DOES NOT FIND THE NEWEST BY TAKING THE LAST OF THESE ... It reads latestCheckpointKey'. ADR-0033 agrees. Read charitably the clause means forensic evidence after the fact, in which case it is the audit-trail argument stated twice with M4.9's name borrowed for weight. The genuinely load-bearing reasons -- the ordered history M7's retention prunes, the record an operator reads, and the audit trail -- are already in the same paragraph and stand without it.
findings.suggestion: Drop the M4.9 clause and keep the audit-trail and M7-retention reasons, which are checkable and sufficient.
findings.failure_scenario: A later reader deciding whether M7's retention may prune the seq-keyed checkpoints, or whether M4.9 may read only the pointer, takes this ADR as the record and concludes M4.9 depends on the seq-keyed objects. It does not, and the alternative's real cost/benefit is then argued from a dependency that never existed -- the 'a correct decision carrying an invented reason' pattern M4.8b2's row records four times.
